The peak residual stress gradually saturates once the weld length exceeds critical values. Consequently, the residual stress comparison across the three floors was only focused on the longitudinal residual stresses among the short and long plate edges. Figure 27 presents the constraint conditions set up for weld models of the three tank floors. The overall pattern of the contour maps of longitudinal stresses in the three floors is similar, comparing Figure 20 and Figure 25 in this report with Figure 91 in the previous report [4]. It is observed that the peak values of longitudinal stresses on long-edge welds, S22 in Figure 20b and Figure 25b, increase from 641 MPa in the 24 m diameter floor, to 686 MPa in the 32 m floor, and 687 MPa in the 39.6 m diameter floors [4]. The highest tensile residual stresses generally occur at a few point locations, such as highly constrained locations or intersections of short-edge and long-edge welds. Within the majority of long-edge weld seams, it was observed that the peak longitudinal residual stress slightly increased with increasing weld pass length, e.g., up to 590 MPa in the 24 m tank, 670 MPa in the 32 m tank, and saturating at 678 MPa in the 39.6 m tanks. Note that the long-edge welds originate from the central line (y = 0), as schematically illustrated in Figure 16b, and progress along the y-axis in either the positive or negative direction simultaneously. Therefore, the long-edge weld pass length increases with increasing floor size. The observed stress trend agrees with the general trend reported in the literature. Figure 28 presents normal distortion contours for the 24, 32, and 39.6 m diameter tank floors. It can be seen that the overall distortion patterns of the three models are similar. As shown in Figure 28, in all three tank floors, long, extended distortion belts (in red color) formed parallel to the x-axis in the long free-of-constraint space between the aligned short edges.
